q: The attractive forces that hold atoms together in compounds are also known as _____.
e: The attractive forces that hold atoms together in compounds are also known as chemical bonds. Intermolecular forces pull neighbouring molecules together, not atoms inside a compound. Nuclear forces hold the nucleus together, not a compound.

q: In atoms, the main shells can be divided into s, p, d, and f subshells which can be filled with _____ electrons, respectively.
e: In atoms, the main shells can be divided into s, p, d, and f subshells which can be filled with 2, 6, 10, and 14 electrons, respectively. A subshell is an s, p, d, or f set of orbitals inside a main shell.

q: The s subshell has only one _____ orbital.
e: The s subshell has only one spherical-shaped orbital. Dumbbell-shaped: a dumbbell shape is a p orbital. Double dumbbell-shaped: a dumbbell shape is a p orbital.

q: There are three _____ p orbitals ($p_x, p_y, p_z$).
e: There are three dumbbell-shaped p orbitals (px, py, pz). Spherical-shaped: a spherical orbital is s. Double dumbbell-shaped: double-dumbbell shapes belong to d orbitals.

q: The five d orbitals have _____ shapes.
e: The five d orbitals have double dumbbell shapes. A spherical orbital is s.

q: According to the _____ principle, electrons are filled in the lower energy atomic orbitals before filling higher energy ones.
e: According to the Aufbau principle, electrons are filled in the lower energy atomic orbitals before filling higher energy ones. Hund's rule spreads electrons through a subshell before pairing. Pauli's: pauli limits one orbital to two opposite-spin electrons.

q: Pauli's exclusion principle states that no more than _____ electrons can occupy the same orbital.
e: Pauli's exclusion principle states that no more than two electrons can occupy the same orbital. Pauli's exclusion principle lets at most two electrons into one orbital, and those two must spin opposite ways.

q: Two electrons in the same orbital must have _____ spins.
e: Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins. An orbital is a region of space where an electron is likely to be found.

q: Hund's rule states that every orbital in a subshell is singly occupied with one electron before any one orbital is _____.
e: Hund's rule states that every orbital in a subshell is singly occupied with one electron before any one orbital is doubly occupied. Empty is not the d-subshell requirement in the transition-metal definition.

q: The electrons in the valence shells of an atom are known as the _____ electrons.
e: The electrons in the valence shells of an atom are known as the valence electrons. Core electrons stay inner and do not bond.

q: For an atom, the number of valence electrons is equal to its _____ in the Periodic Table.
e: For an atom, the number of valence electrons is equal to its group number in the Periodic Table. Period number is the shell, not the valence count. Atomic mass does not count valence electrons.

q: Atoms lose, gain, or share electrons in order to achieve the stable electronic structures of noble gases, which is known as the _____ rule.
e: Atoms lose, gain, or share electrons in order to achieve the stable electronic structures of noble gases, which is known as the octet rule. A duplet is a two-electron shell, not the usual octet. Hund's rule spreads electrons through a subshell before pairing.

q: The octet rule does not apply to _____ elements.
e: The octet rule does not apply to d-block elements. S-block is groups 1 and 2, not the transition block. P-block is groups 13 to 18.

q: Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom to attract the _____ to itself.
e: Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom to attract the shared electrons to itself. Core electrons stay inner and do not bond.

q: Electron affinity is the amount of energy _____ when an electron is added to a gaseous atom.
e: Electron affinity is the amount of energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom. Electron affinity is the energy released when a gaseous atom gains an electron.

q: Ionisation energy is the amount of energy required to _____ an electron from a gaseous atom.
e: Ionisation energy is the amount of energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom. Ionisation energy is the energy you must put in to pull an electron off a gaseous atom.

q: Generally, the higher the first ionisation energy of an element, the _____ is its electronegativity.
e: Generally, the higher the first ionisation energy of an element, the greater is its electronegativity. Greater: ionisation energy is the energy you must put in to pull an electron off a gaseous atom.

q: There are _____ main types of chemical bonding.
e: There are three main types of chemical bonding. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The hydrogen bond is the strongest intermolecular force followed by _____ forces.
e: The hydrogen bond is the strongest intermolecular force followed by van der Waals forces. Van der Waals: intermolecular forces tug neighbouring molecules or ions together; they are not the bonds inside a molecule.

q: Among van der Waals forces, _____ forces are the weakest intermolecular forces that can be found in all substances.
e: Among van der Waals forces, London dispersion forces are the weakest intermolecular forces that can be found in all substances. London dispersion forces are weak temporary-dipole attractions found in every substance.

q: Most bonds are not 100% ionic or 100% covalent, instead most bonds have at least some degree of _____ character.
e: Most bonds are not 100% ionic or 100% covalent, instead most bonds have at least some degree of both ionic and covalent character. Covalent bonding is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: The outermost shell electrons of atoms are the basis for understanding the joining of atoms, and this interaction leads to the forces of attraction known as _____.
e: The outermost shell electrons of atoms are the basis for understanding the joining of atoms, and this interaction leads to the forces of attraction known as chemical bonds. Those outer electrons, the valence electrons, are the ones that actually form bonds.

q: Elements having high electron affinity easily gain electrons, resulting in the formation of the _____.
e: Elements having high electron affinity easily gain electrons, resulting in the formation of the anions. Cations form when atoms lose electrons.

q: Elements having low ionisation energy easily lose electrons, resulting in the formation of the _____.
e: Elements having low ionisation energy easily lose electrons, resulting in the formation of the cations. Anions form when atoms gain electrons.
